title: Graphs
tagline: The most general structure in CS — vertices, edges, and the two traversals that underpin half of all algorithms.

sections.content:
Graphs are the most general data structure in computer science. Where arrays, trees, and linked lists impose strict shape rules, graphs impose almost none: any set of items (**vertices**) connected by any set of relationships (**edges**) forms a graph. Social networks, road maps, dependency graphs, the web itself — all are graphs. Even trees are a special case of a graph (connected, acyclic, directed from root).

Two traversal algorithms — **BFS** and **DFS** — unlock the vast majority of graph problems: shortest paths, connected components, cycle detection, topological sort, and reachability. Choosing the right traversal and the right representation (adjacency list vs matrix) is the skill that separates a competent engineer from one who can solve graph problems under pressure.

sections.title: Cities and Roads
sections.content:
Think of a graph as a map. **Vertices** are cities; **edges** are roads between them. A **directed** graph is a one-way street network — you can drive from A to B but not necessarily B to A. An **undirected** graph allows travel in both directions. A **weighted** graph assigns a cost (distance, travel time, fare) to each road.

Finding the shortest route between two cities is Dijkstra's algorithm on a weighted graph. Checking whether two cities are connected at all is BFS or DFS reachability. Detecting a traffic loop (cycle) in a one-way network uses DFS cycle detection. Every graph problem maps back to one of these fundamental operations.

Graphs are represented in two standard ways. An **adjacency list** maps each vertex to a list of its neighbours. For a graph with V vertices and E edges it uses O(V + E) space and iterates neighbours in O(degree) time — efficient for **sparse** graphs where most vertices have few connections. An **adjacency matrix** is a V×V boolean grid where `matrix[i][j] = 1` means an edge from i to j. It uses O(V²) space but checks whether a specific edge exists in O(1) — efficient for **dense** graphs. Most real-world graphs (social networks, road maps) are sparse, making adjacency lists the default choice.

**Breadth-First Search (BFS)** explores neighbours level by level using a queue. It guarantees the **shortest path** (minimum number of edges) to each vertex in an unweighted graph. Time complexity is O(V + E) — every vertex is enqueued once, every edge is examined once. **Depth-First Search (DFS)** uses a stack (or the call stack recursively) to dive as deep as possible before backtracking. DFS does not guarantee shortest paths but is simpler to implement recursively and is the basis for cycle detection, topological sort, and strongly connected components.

A **directed acyclic graph (DAG)** has directed edges and no cycles. DAGs model task dependencies (build systems, package managers, course prerequisites). **Topological sort** — a DFS-based algorithm — orders vertices so that every directed edge u→v has u before v in the output. It is only possible on DAGs; cycles make topological ordering undefined.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The adjacency list uses a `Map` of arrays — O(V+E) space. BFS tracks `dist` to give shortest hop counts from start. The three-colour DFS (WHITE=unvisited, GRAY=in-stack, BLACK=done) detects back edges in directed graphs — a back edge means a cycle. For undirected graphs a simpler visited-set approach suffices.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs; for weighted graphs use Dijkstra (min-heap + BFS-like relaxation).** When an interview problem mentions 'fewest steps', 'minimum moves', or 'shortest route' with uniform costs — reach for BFS immediately. When edge weights vary, reach for Dijkstra. When edges can have negative weights, use Bellman-Ford.

items: Graphs consist of vertices and edges; they can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, and may contain cycles.
Adjacency lists use O(V+E) space and are efficient for sparse graphs; adjacency matrices use O(V²) space and give O(1) edge lookup for dense graphs.
BFS explores level by level using a queue — guarantees shortest path (min hops) in unweighted graphs — O(V+E).
DFS dives deep using a stack or recursion — used for cycle detection, topological sort, and connected components — O(V+E).
Topological sort orders DAG vertices so all edges go forward — possible only when the graph has no cycles; Kahn's algorithm detects cycles when output length is less than vertex count.

quiz.question: What is the space complexity of an adjacency list for a graph with V vertices and E edges?
quiz.explanation: An adjacency list stores one entry per vertex and one entry per directed edge — O(V) for the vertex list plus O(E) for all the edge entries, totalling O(V+E).

quiz.question: Which graph traversal guarantees the shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph?
quiz.explanation: BFS explores all vertices at distance k before any at distance k+1. The first time BFS reaches a vertex, it has found the shortest hop count path from the source.

quiz.question: What is a directed acyclic graph (DAG)?
options: A graph where every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge
A graph with directed edges and no directed cycles
A graph where all edges are bidirectional
A complete graph where every pair of vertices is connected
quiz.explanation: A DAG has directed edges (arrows) and contains no directed cycles — you cannot follow edges and return to your starting vertex. DAGs model task dependencies, package managers, and course prerequisites.

quiz.question: What does it mean if Kahn's topological sort outputs fewer vertices than the total vertex count?
options: The graph contains a directed cycle
Some vertices have no outgoing edges
quiz.explanation: Kahn's algorithm processes vertices with in-degree 0. If a cycle exists, those vertices never reach in-degree 0 and are never enqueued. The output is shorter than V — a reliable cycle detection signal.

quiz.question: When is an adjacency matrix preferred over an adjacency list?
options: When the graph is sparse (few edges relative to vertices)
When the graph is dense and O(1) edge existence checks are required
When the graph has weighted edges
quiz.explanation: An adjacency matrix offers O(1) edge-existence checks (`matrix[u][v]`), which is valuable for dense graphs. For sparse graphs it wastes O(V²) space storing mostly zeros.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of BFS and DFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
quiz.explanation: Both BFS and DFS visit each vertex once and examine each edge once — O(V+E). For sparse graphs this is much better than O(V²).

quiz.question: In the three-colour DFS cycle detection algorithm (WHITE/GRAY/BLACK), what does a GRAY neighbour indicate?
options: The neighbour has been fully processed
The neighbour has not been visited yet
The neighbour is currently on the DFS stack — a back edge and therefore a cycle
The neighbour is at a greater depth than the current vertex
quiz.explanation: GRAY means the vertex is currently being processed (on the DFS call stack). Encountering a GRAY vertex means you have found an edge from a descendant back to an ancestor — a back edge — which proves a cycle exists.

quiz.question: Which real-world system is most naturally modelled as a weighted directed graph?
options: A road map where roads are one-way and distances vary
A hash table storing user profiles
A binary heap of task priorities
quiz.explanation: A road map with one-way streets is a directed graph (edges have direction) and distances are weights. Dijkstra's algorithm on this graph finds the shortest driving route — the canonical weighted-directed-graph problem.

quiz.question: For a problem asking 'minimum number of moves to transform word A into word B by changing one letter at a time', which algorithm and structure are most appropriate?
options: BFS on an adjacency list (word graph)
Binary search on a sorted word list
quiz.explanation: This is the classic Word Ladder problem. Model words as vertices; add an edge between words that differ by one letter. BFS finds the shortest path (minimum transformations) between source and target words — O(V+E) where V = word count.

quiz.question: A graph has 5 vertices and 4 edges with no cycles and exactly one connected component. What kind of graph is this?
options: A tree — connected acyclic graph with V-1 edges
quiz.explanation: A connected graph with no cycles and exactly V-1 edges is a tree. Trees are a special case of graphs — this is why tree traversal algorithms (pre-order, in-order, post-order) are special cases of DFS.
